name: Vortex-Crucible
description: Vortex-Crucible takes its name from the spinning columns of superheated gas that rise from its volcanic vents, twisting into tight vortices that can reach the upper atmosphere. The surface is a patchwork of obsidian plains and active lava fields, with a ring of supervolcanoes circling the northern hemisphere like a crown of fire. Magnetic anomalies cause compass instruments to spin wildly and create aurora-like displays in the toxic upper atmosphere.

The vortices create a visual spectacle that is as dangerous as it is beautiful, columns of glowing gas spiraling upward in tight corkscrews, their bases rooted in pools of bubbling magma. The magnetic anomalies generate electromagnetic interference that disrupts navigation systems and communications, forcing any approach to rely on visual piloting. The ground trembles in rhythmic pulses, each tremor coinciding with a fresh eruption somewhere along the volcanic ring.

Localized gravity anomalies near the planet's core have been detected, zones where gravitational pull intensifies or weakens unpredictably. These gravity wells appear to shift position over time, suggesting they are linked to the movement of dense material within the mantle. The phenomenon has no established explanation, and some physicists have proposed that Vortex-Crucible may contain a fragment of collapsed stellar matter embedded in its core during formation.

The gravity anomalies make Vortex-Crucible of immense interest to theoretical physicists, who see in them a natural laboratory for studying exotic gravitational effects. The iron and titanium deposits are substantial but secondary to the scientific value. Any expedition must contend with the toxic atmosphere, volcanic activity, electromagnetic interference, and unpredictable gravity, a combination that has earned the planet its reputation as one of the most challenging survey targets in the sector.
